newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran's new president has limited room for manoeuvre.
newsitem.headline: Iran's new president has limited room for manoeuvre.

text.p: Iran's moderate president-elect Mohammad Khatami was swept into office on a tide of desire for change after 18 years of revolution, and the size of his victory will make it hard for the religious establishment to resist domestic reforms, analysts said on Saturday.
But the outlook for foreign policy changes remains more clouded.

Iran's fifth president since Shi'ite Moslem fundamentalists toppled the Shah in 1979 won election by a landslide after his main rival, parliament's conservative speaker Ali Akbar Nateq- Nouri, conceded defeat and sent him a letter of congratulations.
Khatami's victory, with two out of every three votes counted so far from Friday's poll, would have come as a major shock to the Iranian conservative establishment, the analysts said.
Nateq-Nouri was their man and he was confidently predicted to become president despite forecasts of a close contest following a fiercely fought campaign.

"This is Iran's second revolution," said a veteran analyst resident in Tehran. "They may find it hard to swallow but the margin of Khatami's victory is so great that the establishment has to accept the result.
"This is a heavy and massive mandate to reform domestic affairs," the analyst said. "Khatami's government is going to be a very inward-looking government.
"It's a vote by people protesting against the policies of the previous group of people in power," the analyst added.

But Khatami's room for manoeuvre is limited. Although the presidency is Iran's highest elective office it ranks second to that of supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who has paramount authority over all institutions of government.
And the 270-seat Majlis or parliament remains in the control of Nateq-Nouri and like-minded conservatives. When the new president selects his cabinet ministers they must be confirmed by the Majlis.

Khamenei, spiritual successor to the revolution's founder, the late Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, tacitly backed the loser and sent coded signals to the electorate to vote for the "best qualified" candidate who could "stand against America and those who want to impose their will on our nation".
His word remains sacrosanct and unchallengeable in all affairs of state including foreign policy, as Iran's veteran Foreign Minister Ali Akbar Velayati noted.
Velayati, the voice of Iran in world capitals for the past 17 years, publicly backed Nateq-Nouri and was tipped to become vice-president if the speaker won.
He said last Sunday the principles of Iran's foreign policy would not change whatever the election outcome because these had been defined by the supreme leader since the beginning of the revolution.

Velayati held out little hope for better relations with the West. Ties with the United States were severed in 1980 at the height of the U.S. embassy hostage crisis in Tehran and have sunk ever lower in the intervening years with the U.S. downing of an Iran Air Airbus over the Gulf in 1988 and the Clinton administration policy of isolating Iran through trade sanctions because of alleged support for "terrorism".
Lately Iran has become embroiled in a noisy row with the European Union over German court charges that Iran's top leaders were involved in political assassinations in Berlin.
The charges enraged the Iranian leadership and were vehemently denied. All 15 of the EU's ambassadors to Tehran are absent from the Iranian capital waiting for tempers to cool.

Khatami is known to have a more open-minded approach to the West than most in power here. He says Iran could expedite domestic progress by learning from the West, a controversial viewpoint in a country where hatred of the United States -- the "Great Satan" of Iranian demonology -- is an act of revolutionary faith.
